items.article_search_text: Inside Formula One team dynamics, controversial teammate clashes, governance, and the McLaren-Norris vs. Piastri Singapore sprint incident examined. Formula 1: McLaren’s Papaya rules under scrutiny once again after Norris-Piastri Singapore Sprint crash center McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in action during the Sprint race at Singapore. REUTERS REUTERS https://ss-i.thgim.com/public/incoming/ktylc7/article71602112.ece/alternates/FREE_1200/2026-10-10T103449Z_71507345_UP1EMAA0TDWYA_RTRMADP_3_MOTOR-F1-SINGAPORE.JPG JAKUB PORZYCKI Formula One F1 - Singapore Grand Prix - Marina Bay Street Circuit, Singapore - October 10, 2026 McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in action during the sprint race REUTERS/Jakub Porzycki The collision cost McLaren eight points and exposed the limits of its race-hard, race-clean philosophy, with the team now facing a crucial Constructors’ Championship fight against Red Bull. CHENNAI Formula One is a team sport. Or so they say. Some teams and drivers fully adhere to that philosophy. But those following the sport day in and day out know the adage is often a farce. There is nothing more supreme than the drivers’ title, and seasons are often recollected based on who won the championship that year. Right from the historic Alain Prost-Ayrton Senna tangle at the Casio Triangle chicane during the 1989 Japanese Grand Prix, flashpoints between teammates have become one of the intriguing aspects of the highest tier of single-seater racing. Since that clash that decided the World Championship, many such skirmishes within the same team have occurred — Sebastian Vettel and Mark Webber in Turkey in 2010, Nico Rosberg and Lewis Hamilton in Spain in 2016, Max Verstappen and Daniel Ricciardo in Azerbaijan in 2018, to name a few. This season’s prime moment of controversy came during the Sprint Race ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix. The final podium spot was on the line as the two McLarens chased Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc. READ: McLaren puts five historic F1 cars linked to Senna, Hamilton and Norris up for sale https://sportstar.thehindu.com/motorsport/f1-mclaren-five-historic-cars-sale-senna-hamilton-norris-brad-pitt-latest-racing/article71601033.ece#google_vignette The scarlet-red car was within touching distance of Oscar Piastri in the lead McLaren. Heading into Turn 5 on the final lap, defending champion Lando Norris attempted a chancy move down the inside of his teammate. The risky endeavour only resulted in a tangle which sent both the cars spinning. Piastri lurched into the barriers, forcing him to retire, while his teammate limped home in eighth to get the last available point. “It was a big gap [and] I went for it. I have the right to do that,” was Norris’ first reaction after the incident. “There was a big opportunity at Turn 5. The gap closed [a] bit more than I would have liked. Obviously, I’ve had to back out of it because the gap was closing, so I’ve had to try and avoid the incident, and obviously there still was one,” the driver of Car No. 1 said. Piastri argued that he had not seen his teammate make the dive up the inside. “I looked behind into the corner and saw he was a reasonable way behind for a corner like that,” he said. This is not the first time the two teammates have come together. At last year’s Canadian Grand Prix, the two title protagonists collided heading into the start-finish straight, and once again it was Norris running into the back of his teammate. ALSO READ: F2 CEO expects West Asia races to go ahead with title still up for grabs https://sportstar.thehindu.com/motorsport/formula-two-formula-one-west-asia-grand-prix-expected-to-happen/article71592464.ece Although there wasn’t much in it for the team this time, compared to the championship challenge last year, team principal Andrea Stella wasn’t pleased. “Disappointed as a team principal by a situation that is absolutely not acceptable, because it caused material damage to the team, and every member of the team knows that the team’s interest comes before any personal interest,” the Italian said post-race. The collision once again brings the team’s ‘Papaya rules’ into question. McLaren CEO Zak Brown defined the term as: “It’s your teammate; race him hard, race him clean, don’t touch.” One of the key elements of the code is to ensure fairness between the two teammates. But very often, it is simply difficult to point fingers at one driver for a clash involving the two. Even in Singapore, the blame cannot be solely placed at Norris’ feet. The Briton argues that his front wheel was level with Piastri’s rearview mirror at the apex, and that gives him the right to go for the overtake. During the tense title fights between Rosberg and Hamilton, Mercedes put together a ‘rules of engagement’ to clearly demarcate how the drivers should race, with the team stepping in only as a last resort. While the document did help reduce the number of incidents, it couldn’t prevent the first-lap crash in Barcelona, which resulted in both drivers getting a dressing down at the team’s headquarters in Brackley, after which the rules were further strengthened. Rosberg also revealed later that the drivers had to contribute to the cost of damages if it occurred during a tussle with a teammate. McLaren is not in contention for either championship this year but is in a serious fight for second place in the Constructors’ standings. The eight points lost due to the tussle leave the team just nine ahead of Red Bull in third place, and with Verstappen hitting his stride in the latter part of the season, the odds are stacked against the defending teams’ champion. A more definitive method of dealing with these incidents will only help the team maximise its points if it hopes for a title challenge next year.

items.article_search_text: McLaren demands greater teamwork from Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri after their Singapore sprint collision cost points and damaged the team's championship campaign. McLaren has intensified discussions with Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri following their collision in the Singapore Grand Prix sprint, as the team seeks to protect its constructors' championship position. The incident occurred on the final lap when Norris attempted to overtake Piastri at Turn 5, sending both cars spinning and leaving the team with fewer points, additional repair costs and renewed questions about its policy of treating both drivers equally.Piastri retired after hitting the barriers, while Norris recovered to finish eighth. According to Autosport, the collision cost McLaren valuable championship points and forced mechanics to undertake additional work, including replacing Piastri's gearbox. The stewards took no further action over the incident.McLaren team principal Andrea Stella described the crash as unacceptable, emphasizing that individual ambitions must not undermine the team's collective objectives. The team's position has become more urgent as Red Bull closes in on third place in the constructors' standings.“It is serious because the damage for the team is material. We are in a close fight in the championship. We had the ambition to challenge Ferrari and we have an ambition to finish ahead of Red Bull, and this is a problem to finish ahead,” Stella said, according to Autosport.Stella said the ongoing discussions would focus on preventing similar incidents rather than assigning blame. McLaren wants both drivers to understand that protecting the team's interests must take priority during on-track battles.“The conversations that we are having they are not finished, but it's not because we need to go back discussing if Lando was alongside Oscar – that's not the interesting bit,” Stella said, according to Motorsport.com.McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown delivered a firmer message after the race. Speaking to Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle, Brown made clear that the team would not tolerate a repeat of the collision, particularly with the constructors' championship battle tightening.“Oh yeah. That was a 'don't do that again'. And we didn't say please. That's an order,” Brown said, according to Motorsport.com.Norris initially defended his attempt, arguing that he had the right to pursue the available gap. However, by the end of the Grand Prix weekend, the reigning world champion accepted responsibility and acknowledged that his decision had harmed the team.“I can't attempt what I did. I should never have attempted it in the first place, even if the move was on. I simply have to think more about the team that I represent more than myself.It was a mistake on my part, I let down the team. I've also apologised to all of them and I owe them all an apology and we'll do better next time,” Norris said, according to Motorsport.com.Norris also demonstrated a more cooperative approach during Sunday's race by offering to help Piastri overtake Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari. McLaren did not need to act on the offer, as Piastri finished fifth, one place behind Norris in fourth.According to Motorsport.com, McLaren sits third in the 2026 constructors' standings with 339 points, trailing Ferrari by 105 points and leading Red Bull by just seven. The team heads to the United States Grand Prix in Austin facing continued pressure to maintain its position.

items.article_search_text: The McLaren CEO assures that the Australian is recovering his confidence and performance after a complicated start to the season. Zak Brown has launched a message of optimism about Oscar Piastri's future at McLaren [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/mclaren]. The British team's CEO considers that the Australian driver is recovering the confidence and performance that made him one of the most promising drivers on the grid, after an especially complicated start to the 2026 season: "I think so; he is becoming the driver I know again. With these cars, the field has gotten a bit mixed up, right? Lewis Hamilton is getting more out of the Ferrari now. George Russell got more out of the car last year than Kimi Antonelli; that has changed. I think these cars are so complex that some drivers have adapted a little faster than others, but I like what I'm seeing from Oscar; he feels more confident and in control. I like where our two drivers are now," Brown declared at the Friday press conference in Singapore. Piastri's season has been marked by his struggle to adapt to the new generation of cars. After finishing third in the drivers' championship in 2025, the Australian has struggled to extract consistent performance from the MCL40. Although he has achieved two podiums this year, he has not matched the pace of his teammate, Lando Norris, who has added two Grand Prix victories and has beaten him in qualifying in 11 of the 17 rounds contested so far. Stella and Norris’s Maturity: 'He Set Aside His Interests' [https://deweb-519a7.b-cdn.net/post-images/fc709052-dc86-4aeb-b701-0a7c81d49ea2.jpeg] Stella and Norris’s Maturity: 'He Set Aside His Interests' The McLaren director praises the champion for helping Piastri finish fifth in Singapore after the crash that took them out of the fight. [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/stella-and-norris-s-maturity-he-set-aside-his-interests] Andrea Stella [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/stella-and-norris-s-maturity-he-set-aside-his-interests], McLaren team boss, had already explained that Piastri was having difficulties driving by "pure instinct" in certain conditions, a situation that the driver himself acknowledged before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix: "Many of the things that had worked for me previously don't seem to work this year, so it's about trying to find others that do. I'm making progress on that, but it is not as simple as finding a direction that works for you all the time. You need to adapt and change things constantly," Piastri explained. Despite the ups and downs, the Australian has shown signs of recovery in the last races, at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia he finished sixth after a complicated afternoon in Sepang where a decision to start on medium tires in wet conditions forced him to enter the pits earlier than planned, however he showed himself satisfied with his own performance, later at the Singapore Grand Prix, he finished fifth after an eventful race, in which he retired from the Sprint due to a crash with Norris on the last lap and suffered a slow puncture on Sunday that forced him to make an unscheduled stop, despite everything, he managed to overtake Hamilton on the last lap to take fifth position. Ranking the Best 25-and-Under Current F1 Drivers [https://deweb-519a7.b-cdn.net/post-images/1df5bb79-8505-4430-a7df-372c770a407f.jpeg] Ranking the Best 25-and-Under Current F1 Drivers Two obvious names are at the top of the best 25-and-under Formula 1 drivers. But how does the rest of the list shape up? [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/ranking-the-best-25-and-under-current-f1-drivers] "It was quite reasonable, I would say; I think we simply didn't have enough pace. We couldn't follow Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc; I think Kimi was also a little faster than us. There wasn't much we could do beyond where we finished," Piastri reflected. Brown, for his part, trusts that McLaren can maintain its progress in the final stretch of the season: "The objective is to arrive at every weekend with the possibility of winning; we feel more in control of things than in the last races, and we won the two before those. It shows how competitive the sport is and how fast the top four teams, and the whole grid, move up and down the competitiveness ladder. Our objective is to try to arrive at every race weekend and win, but that is easier said than done," Brown concluded.

McLaren Team Principal Andrea Stella has identified what he believes is the root of Oscar Piastri‘s ongoing struggles to find success in the 2026 season. Stella said that he believes Piastri’s ‘signature’ clean driving style has not matched the MCL40 as well as its predecessor. The Australian earned seven Grand Prix victories in 2025, leading […] Motorsport Week is an independent, FIA accredited motorsport website delivering the latest Formula 1, Formula E, GP2, GP3, WEC, IndyCar, Nascar, Formula 3, WRC, WRX, DTM, IMSA and MotoGP news and results. McLaren Team Principal Andrea Stella has identified what he believes is the root of Oscar Piastri 's ongoing struggles to find success in the 2026 season . Stella said that he believes Piastri's 'signature' clean driving style has not matched the MCL40 as well as its predecessor. The Australian earned seven Grand Prix victories in 2025, leading the Driver's Championship for much of the season before losing out to teammate Lando Norris. However so far in 2026, Piastri has only two podiums to his name, with the most recent being in Miami back in May. Stella thinks that Piastri is simply taking longer to adapt his driving style to the new era of cars, as he explained to the media in Singapore. "The car needs quite a lot of effort to deliver lap time, and it requires a level of intensity in the driving input, which is much superior to last year," he said. "This is something that took some time for the drivers to get comfortable. Well, comfortable is wrong, but to get to understand, and it's also one of the reasons why Oscar almost looks like he lost some of the competitiveness compared to Lando. "We were discussing what is happening with Oscar, and I've always said that that was a technical matter. Oscar just needed to understand how to force the car to do some things and sort of abandon the fact that driving fast will not necessarily mean driving clean. "Instead, probably the signature of Oscar, when we have seen him fast in the past, was that he was clean. It was really good data to see. "It was very repeatable, and it was fast. With this car, all these things together don't seem to happen very often. So it's a lot of work for the drivers." Oscar Piastri has only managed two podiums so far this season Stella not expecting upgrades miracles for either Oscar Piastri or Lando Norris McLaren has confirmed that it will bring a new upgrade package at some point before the end of the season, but Stella does not believe this will make it easier to drive. "I don't expect that what's coming to the car will improve this characteristic. "I think we need something more fundamental than simply adding some downforce to the car, like it's happening in the coming races, without fundamentally changing some further aspect, which we are addressing longer term, I would say with the MCL41 for 2027." items.article_search_text: Lando Norris apologized after colliding with Oscar Piastri in Singapore, while Andrea Stella reaffirmed McLaren's commitment to equal treatment and team unity. McLaren has reaffirmed its commitment to equal treatment for Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri after their collision in the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race exposed tensions between individual ambition and team priorities. The incident on the final lap cost the team valuable points, prompting team principal Andrea Stella to demand greater unity from both drivers before the main race.Norris attempted to overtake Piastri at Turn Five, but the two McLaren cars made contact and spun. Piastri hit the barriers and retired, while Norris recovered to finish eighth, scoring one point. According to BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson, the team lost the opportunity to collect nine points from the sprint.Norris initially defended his decision to attempt the pass, arguing that the move was permitted under racing guidelines. However, he later accepted responsibility, acknowledging that his personal ambitions should not have taken priority over McLaren's collective interests.After the race, Norris admitted the attempt was unnecessary and apologized to the team. He also offered to help Piastri during the Grand Prix when the Australian was trying to recover from a slow puncture and an additional pit stop.Speaking after the Grand Prix, Norris explained that Piastri had been unfortunate with the puncture and that his own car had experienced problems. With several cars separating them and little realistic opportunity for Norris to catch Kimi Antonelli, he believed helping his teammate offered a better chance of maximizing McLaren's points.Stella welcomed the change in approach, saying the team had already discussed the sprint collision with both drivers. He emphasized that the central issue was not whether Norris had been alongside Piastri during the attempted pass, but whether both drivers consistently prioritized the team over individual interests.The McLaren team principal maintained that the organization would continue treating its drivers fairly and would not abandon its policy of equal status. He also said further discussions were necessary to strengthen cooperation between the drivers and the wider team.Former Haas team principal Guenther Steiner criticized Norris's decision during an appearance on The Red Flags Podcast, describing the incident as a mistake inconsistent with the judgment expected from a world champion. Steiner also praised Stella's handling of the situation, arguing that Norris ultimately recognized the unnecessary risk and the importance of his subsequent response.Despite the sprint collision, McLaren recovered in Sunday's Grand Prix, with Norris finishing fourth and Piastri fifth. According to Formula1.com, the result restored the positions the pair had effectively lost through the previous day's incident and gave the team a stronger points return.Stella said McLaren's strategy had been designed to maximize the drivers' opportunities at the start. Both cars began on soft tires because the team believed the medium compound could leave them vulnerable to losing positions and being forced into an early pit stop.McLaren subsequently extended its opening stint in the hope that a Safety Car would reduce the time lost during a pit stop. No Safety Car appeared, and the team ultimately finished behind Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes, according to Formula1.com.Stella considered fourth and fifth the best realistic result on performance, although he acknowledged that Norris might have had an opportunity to challenge Antonelli for a podium position under different circumstances. He also pointed to planned car upgrades as a potential improvement for the team's upcoming races.Motorsport.com reported that Norris and Piastri collected 22 points combined in the Grand Prix after scoring only one point in the sprint. The result gave McLaren an opportunity to move forward after a difficult weekend while the team continued addressing the lessons from the collision.

Jack has been obsessed with cars from before he can even remember, and has a vested interest and knowledge of F1 from the 1980s, 90s and 2000s, his heroes being Damon Hill and Michael Schumacher McLaren CEO Zak Brown has revealed that both Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were handed a stern warning after their last-lap collision in the Formula 1 Sprint Race in Singapore. Running fourth and fifth in the 20-lap prelude to Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix , Norris began swarming all over the back of his team. This culminated in a risky move on a partly damp track with Norris sticking his MCL40 up the inside of the Australian at Turn 5. Piastri's sister car was prodded sideways, with both spinning and eventually facing backwards, and almost collected by the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson. Norris got going again and finished eighth for one point, whereas Piastri retired on the spot. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Motorsport Week (@motorsportweek) The reigning World Champion apologised for the manoeuvre but also defended the attempt to overtake his teammate, although showed more contrition after the race on Sunday. Ahead of the race, in which both men finished - coincidentally - fourth and fifth [with Norris the leading car], Brown was approached by Sky Sports F1 commentator Martin Brundle on his infamous grid walk. "I’m going to imagine [there were] some fairly stern words last night to your drivers, who managed to trip over each other," Brundle commented. "Oh yeah," Brown admitted. "That was a ‘don’t do that again.’ And we didn’t say 'please'. 'That’s an order'." The move cost McLaren eight World Championship points, as the race for 'best of the rest' in the Constructors' Championship hots up between the Woking-based squad, Ferrari and Red Bull. "Yeah. You can’t have that," Brown added. "It was an unnecessary result for the team when a lot of pressure is on, and we’re trying to catch Ferrari and Red Bull’s not far behind. "We learn from it. I think there are some things they definitely could have done differently. Maybe a few things we could have done a little bit differently. So you learn." items.article_search_text: Young Guns Part 2: Oscar Piastri vs Pedro Acosta, the Off-Road Rematch Formula 1 driver Oscar Piastri and MotoGP rider Pedro Acosta are back. Two years after their karting showdown, the Quad Lock athletes have traded Grand Prix machinery for identical off-road buggies in Young Guns Part 2. Three challenges, one motocro Young Guns Part 2: Oscar Piastri vs Pedro Acosta, the Off-Road Rematch Formula 1 driver Oscar Piastri and MotoGP rider Pedro Acosta are back. Two years after their karting showdown, the Quad Lock athletes have traded Grand Prix machinery for identical off-road buggies in Young Guns Part 2. Three challenges, one motocross track, and one winner. Where it started: Young Guns Part 1 In 2024, Quad Lock brought Piastri and Acosta together for the first Young Guns film. It was a karting challenge in France, with Acosta driving a kart for the first time. Piastri came out on top. A lot has happened since. Piastri is now a nine-time Formula 1 Grand Prix winner with the McLaren Mastercard Formula 1 Team. Acosta won his first MotoGP Grand Prix in Austria in September 2026 and is one of the championship’s standout young talents. F1 vs MotoGP on dirt For Part 2, the pair left the tarmac behind. Young Guns Part 2 was filmed on 14 August 2026 at Monti MX, a motocross circuit in the hills above Menton on the French Riviera. The track is hard-packed, rutted and full of jumps. Piastri and Acosta raced matching Segway Super Villain buggies, which took both of them out of their usual disciplines. Four wheels suit Piastri, and dirt suits Acosta. Neither of them races buggies. “Last time it was karting, which is pretty much home turf for me, so I had a bit of an advantage,” said Piastri. “This time Pedro probably had the edge, with the dirt and the jumps. I’ll let people watch and decide who handled it better.” “I always have a good time with Oscar,” said Acosta. “We laughed a lot making the first video, and this one was the same. Being on the dirt with the buggies was something different for us, and the track at Monti is amazing.” Hosted by Charley Boorman Long-time Quad Lock ambassador, adventure rider and TV presenter Charley Boorman hosts the showdown. He takes the pair through each challenge and catches the moments between runs. The film combines on-board cameras, drones and trackside footage with candid moments away from a Grand Prix weekend. It is Quad Lock’s most ambitious production to date. Quad Lock mounts, put to the test The phones in Young Guns Part 2 weren’t props. Both buggies ran Quad Lock mounts, and the phones were part of the challenges themselves, so they had to take the vibration, impacts and jumps of a full motocross circuit. “Our product is integrated into the challenges because that is where it belongs,” said Dom Storey, Global Head of Sports Marketing at Quad Lock. Every Quad Lock mount uses the Dual Stage Lock, which is built to keep your phone secure when the terrain gets rough. The gear in the film Quad Lock Roll Cage Mount Mounts your phone to the roll cage tubing of a buggy, UTV or side-by-side, with your screen in view. Quad Lock 360 Range A modular system of arms and heads that lets you set your phone at the angle and position you want. Quad Lock MAG Case range Phone cases with the Quad Lock interface built in, ready to lock onto any Quad Lock mount. Quad Lock Action Camera Adaptors Lets you run an action camera on your Quad Lock mounts to capture your own ride. SHOP OFF-ROAD MOUNTS FAQs What is Young Guns Part 2? Where was Young Guns Part 2 filmed? At Monti MX, a motocross circuit in the hills above Menton on the French Riviera, on 14 August 2026. Who won Young Guns Part 1? Oscar Piastri won the karting challenge in Young Guns Part 1, which was filmed in 2024 and was Acosta’s first time driving a kart. Who hosts Young Guns Part 2? items.article_search_text: Lando Norris has accepted the blame for colliding with Oscar Piastri in the Sprint at the Singapore Grand Prix on Saturday; watch every session of the United States GP in Austin on October 23-25, live on Sky Sports F1 Lando Norris says he let McLaren down and has taken responsibility for his collision with Oscar Piastri in the Sprint at the Singapore Grand Prix. Norris and Piastri made contact on the last lap of Saturday's shortened race when battling for fourth, which the stewards did not penalise either driver for. However, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella labelled the incident as "not acceptable" while Norris was not keen to talk about the collision on Saturday and told Sky Sports F1 : "As a team we all spoke about it. I apologised but that's all you need to know." Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺 However, following his fourth-place finish in Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix, Norris changed his tune when speaking to the written media. "It's pretty straightforward. I can't attempt what I did. I should never have attempted in the first place, even if the move was on. I've got to think of the team that I represent more than myself," he said. "It was a mistake on my part, and I let down the team. I've also apologised to all of them, I owe them all an apology, and I will do better next time." Stella: Conversations with drivers not finished During Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix, Norris asked several times if he could aid team-mate Piastri in any way during the closing stages of the race. Piastri was attempting to catch and overtake Lewis Hamilton at the time of the radio calls, suggesting Norris was querying whether he should back up the Ferrari driver. In the end, Piastri overtook Hamilton without any help to finish fifth behind Norris. Stella says he was "very encouraged" by Norris' willingness to aid his team-mate but more talks will be held before the United States Grand Prix in Austin next weekend. "We are aligned as to how we want to lead this team forward in a joint effort between the team and the drivers," he said. "The conversations that we are having, they are not finished but it's not because we need to go back discussing if Lando was alongside Oscar, that's not the interesting bit. "For me the interesting bit is a reflection that all the stakeholders, the team, the drivers will have to make around leading together the team, embracing constantly from inside the cockpit the interest of the team, as something that is superior to any particular singular individual interest. "While the conversations from this point of view, they are not concluded and there's more we can do to become a more united and even stronger team, I'm pleased that Lando at some stage in the race adopted this way of thinking. "This is what I expect as a team principal, this is what the 1000 people that work at McLaren expect from our drivers so it's good that we read this example. I expect definitely more of that in the future, independently of the fact that they will be heard in the radio, or they will happen behind the closed door in every meeting or in the way we approach our race plan."
